item.title: Safe Portfolio Learning from Untrusted Predictions: Signed Trust, Abstention, and Cross-Universe Polarity Failure
item.description: arXiv:2611.04826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Portfolio use of machine predictions must often proceed while the predictions' economic direction, reliability, and timing remain untrusted, and while feedback from overlapping multi-period positions arrives with delay. A controller chooses among Safe, Follow, and Reverse portfolio actions, so signal orientation is learned rather than assumed. A share-adaptive master updates action probabilities from matured Safe-relative rewards, an evidence gate can abstain by transferring unsupported directional probability to Safe, a delayed collateral budget reserves worst-case loss capacity before exposure is funded, and a protected split account caps the capital adaptive decisions may touch. The architecture carries a dual certificate, tracking regret against switching action sequences under delay and one-sided intervention, together with a pathwise collateral safety bound that holds when predictions fail. On a 24-stock development universe a conservative prediction-assisted overlay stays near equal-weight performance at a fraction of the turnover. On a frozen 82-stock holdout, the pre-specified Reverse orientation fails to outperform Equal Weight; a separately labeled post-holdout diagnostic shows that permanently flipping the sign to Follow also does not recover a return edge. Under the post-holdout controller, protected wealth remains within 15.9 basis points of the Safe benchmark throughout. The contribution is safe adaptive use of untrusted predictions, not demonstrated alpha.

item.title: Long-term yields of short-rate models as Feynman-Kac ground states: a variational quantum eigensolver with single-setting energy estimation on two NISQ platforms
item.description: arXiv:2611.01855v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that the long-term yield of a short-rate model is the ground-state energy of a Schrodinger operator obtained from the Feynman-Kac bond-pricing equation, so that it can be computed by a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We treat the Vasicek, Cox-Ingersoll-Ross and Black-Karasinski models; the last has no closed form. Calibrated monthly to the U.S. Treasury curve from 1985 to 2026, the long-term yield follows the 30-year yield with an in-sample correlation of 0.98. The Hamiltonian is stoquastic, so its ground state is positive and the energy can be estimated from computational-basis samples with a single measurement setting. On ibm_cleveland, gate noise appears mainly as bit flips of the high-order qubits. A bit-flip deconvolution with a tail set fixed by a WKB criterion, combined with readout mitigation and zero-noise extrapolation, gives four-qubit estimates within 33-125 bp of the grid ground-state energies for all three models, and within 23-67 bp for Treasury-calibrated parameters. On IonQ Forte Enterprise the same analysis reduces the error in the same proportions. On the same circuits, a Pauli-measurement VQE deviates by 791-1,129 bp, so the single-setting estimator gives about ten times smaller errors with one setting instead of nine. An on-device VQE converges from 4,939 bp to 130 bp.

item.title: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity
item.description: arXiv:2310.12255v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This article advocates the development of a decentralized exchange protocol for Ethereum based on Walrasian equilibrium. Building on previous work (arXiv:2111.02719, arXiv:2210.04929), it develops a mathematical framework that incorporates liquidity from independent automated market makers (AMMs). Trade orders are represented by continuous monotonic pairwise supply functions and external AMMs are represented by concave swap functions. Under a connectivity condition, we establish the existence of a common clearing-price vector and external swaps that jointly fulfill the prescribed orders while leaving a nonnegative surplus of every token. External AMMs execute ordinary swaps according to their own pricing rules, including swap fees. For the selected clearing-price vector, the prescribed external swaps maximize the value of the batch surplus. We also establish structural properties of equilibrium, including invariance of individual net trades across equilibria, and formulate equilibrium computation as a convex optimization problem. We then outline Walraswap, an exchange protocol for Ethereum with off-chain batch construction and on-chain settlement. Its proposed governance and solver accountability mechanisms aim to encourage public order disclosure and discourage censorship. The protocol design explores how the mathematical construction could support decentralized trading with reduced opportunities for maximal extractable value.
item.dc:creator: Sergio A. Yuhjtman

item.title: Partially Active Automated Market Makers
item.description: arXiv:2602.09887v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a new class of automated market maker (AMM), the \emph{partially active automated market maker} (PA-AMM). PA-AMM divides its reserves into two parts, the active and the passive parts, and uses only the active part for trading. At the top of every block, such a division is done again to keep the active reserves always being \(\lambda\)-portion of total reserves, where \(\lambda \in (0, 1]\) is an activeness parameter. We show that this simple mechanism reduces adverse selection costs, measured by loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR), and thereby improves the wealth of liquidity providers (LPs) relative to plain constant-function market makers (CFMMs). As a trade-off, the asset weights within a PA-AMM pool may deviate from their target weights implied by its invariant curve. Motivated by the optimal index-tracking problem literature, we also propose and solve an optimization problem that balances such deviation and the reduction of LVR.
item.dc:creator: Sunghun Ko, Seungwon Jeong

item.title: A mathematical study of the excess growth rate
item.description: arXiv:2510.25740v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The excess growth rate, defined as the gap in Jensen's inequality for the logarithm, is a fundamental functional in portfolio theory. In this paper, we present a mathematical study motivated by information theory. We begin by establishing its properties and showing that it has rich connections with information-theoretic concepts such as the Helmholtz free energy, L. Campbell's measure of average code length and large deviations. Our main results consist of three axiomatic characterization theorems of the excess growth rate, in terms of (i) the relative entropy, (ii) the gap in Jensen's inequality, and (iii) the logarithmic divergence that generalizes the Bregman divergence. Furthermore, we study maximization of the excess growth rate and compare it with Kelly's growth optimal portfolio. Our results not only provide theoretical justifications of the significance of the excess growth rate, but also establish new connections between information theory and quantitative finance.
